en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 41.1 (SN 41.1, PTS SN iv 281) 1. Cittavagga Saṁyojana Sutta: Fetters “Bhikkhus, there are these five lower fetters. What five? They are: identity view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ill will. These are the five lower fetters. “Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters. What five? They are: lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance. These are the five higher fetters.”
On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.
Now at that time, after their meal, on returning from their alms round, a number of elder bhikkhus had gathered and were seated together in the assembly hall when this discussion arose among them:
"Friends, as for these things called 'fetters' and 'things that fetter,' are they different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they identical in meaning and different only in phrasing?"
In this regard, some elder bhikkhus declared:
"Friend, 'fetter' and 'things that fetter'—these things are different in meaning and different in phrasing.
Some other elder bhikkhus declared:
“Friend, ‘fetter’ and ‘things that fetter’—these states have the same meaning; only the phrasing is different.
Now at that time, the householder Citta had arrived at Migapathaka on some business.

The householder Citta heard that a discussion concerning this matter had arisen among a number of elder bhikkhus as they were sitting together and assembled in the pavilion after their meal, having returned from their almsround: [the discourse continues].

“Friend, are these things—namely, ‘the fetter’ and ‘the phenomena that are subject to fettering’—different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and different only in phrasing?
On this matter, some elder bhikkhus replied:
“Friend, these things—namely, ‘the fetter’ and ‘the phenomena that are subject to fettering’—are indeed different in meaning and different in phrasing.”
Some elder bhikkhus had declared thus:
"Friend, 'fetter' and 'things that fetter'—these states have the same meaning; only the phrasing is different.

Then Citta the householder approached those elder bhikkhus; having approached and paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Citta the householder said this to the elder bhikkhus:

“I have heard this, Bhante: after returning from their almsround following the meal, a number of elder bhikkhus were sitting together and assembled in the pavilion when this discussion arose among them:

‘Friend, regarding what is called “fetter” (saṁyojana) or what are called “things that fetter” (saṁyojaniyā dhammā)—are these things different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and only the phrasing is different?
Some elder bhikkhus answered thus:”
“Friend, whether one says ‘the fetter’ or ‘the things that fetter,’ these phenomena are different both in meaning and in phrasing.
Some elder bhikkhus had explained it thus: “Friend, whether one says ‘the fetter’ or ‘the things that fetter,’ these phenomena are identical in meaning; only the phrasing is different.
“It is so, householder.”
“Venerable sir, whether one says ‘fetter’ or ‘things that fetter,’ these phenomena are different both in meaning and in phrasing.
Therefore, venerable sir, I shall give you a simile;
for by means of a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what has been said.”
“Venerable sir, suppose there were a black ox and a white ox tied together by a single rope or yoke.
Would one who spoke thus:
‘The black ox is the fetter for the white ox; the white ox is the fetter for the black ox’—would he be speaking rightly?”
“No, householder.
It is not that the black ox is the fetter for the white ox, nor is the white ox the fetter for the black ox;
rather, that by which they are bound together—whether by a single rope or a yoke—that is the fetter there.”
“In the same way, Bhante, the eye is not the fetter of forms, nor are forms the fetter of the eye;
rather, the desire and lust that arise there dependent upon both of them—that is the fetter there.
The ear is not the fetter of sounds …”
The nose is not a fetter for odors, nor are odors a fetter for the nose;
the tongue is not a fetter for tastes, nor are tastes a fetter for the tongue; the body is not a fetter for tangibles, nor are tangibles a fetter for the body.
And whatever desire and lust arise there dependent upon both of those—that is the fetter there.
The mind is not the fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena the fetter of the mind;
rather, whatever desire and lust arise there dependent upon both of those—that is the fetter there.”
“It is a gain for you, householder, it is well-gained by you, householder,
that your eye of wisdom ranges over the profound word of the Buddha. Thus [ends] the first [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 41.2 (SN 41.2, PTS SN iv 283) 1. Cittavagga Paṭhamaisidattasutta (The First Discourse to Isidatta) Then the householder Isidatta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Householder, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own purpose, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. What are these four? Here, householder, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Householder, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own purpose, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the householder Isidatta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One explained the Dhamma in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for as long as life shall last. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of stream-entry. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of once-returning, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of once-returning. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of once-returning. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of non-returning. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of non-returning. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained final knowledge, or those who have entered upon the way to final knowledge. “I, venerable sir, am one who has entered upon the way to final knowledge. When this was said, the householder Isidatta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned... even so has the Blessed One explained the Dhamma in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for as long as life shall last. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of stream-entry. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of once-returning, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of once-returning. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of once-returning.

“Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, or those who have entered upon the way to the fruit of non-returning. “I, venerable sir, am one who has attained the fruit of non-returning. “Householder, those who previously were followers of other sects and later become followers of the Tathāgata, they are of two kinds: either those who have attained final knowledge, or those who have entered upon the way to final knowledge. “I, venerable sir, am one who has entered upon the way to final knowledge. When this was said, the householder Isidatta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned... even so has the Blessed One explained the Dhamma in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth, for as long as life shall last. [The Blessed One accepted him. Then the householder Isidatta, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the householder Isidatta went to the householder Pūraṇa Kassapa, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the householder Isidatta said to the householder Pūraṇa Kassapa: “Friend Kassapa, I have seen the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. “But did you hear anything spoken by the Blessed One? “Yes, friend, I heard something spoken by the Blessed One. “What did you hear, friend? “Friend, the Blessed One said: ‘Householder, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own purpose, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. What are these four? Here, householder, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [and so on] ...he is liberated through final knowledge. “Friend, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is well-expounded, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is clear, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is flawless, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is unadulterated, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is immaculate, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is leading to liberation, and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is expounded by one who is himself liberated! [The rest of the discourse proceeds with the same exchange regarding the other teachers, culminating in: “Friend, it is wonderful, it is marvelous how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is well-expounded... and how the Dhamma of the ascetic Gotama is expounded by one who is himself liberated! “Friend, let us go to the ascetic Gotama and declare our adherence to his Dhamma. “Enough, friend, do not go to the ascetic Gotama and declare our adherence to his Dhamma. [Isidatta repeats his request three times, and each time Pūraṇa Kassapa refuses. Then the householder Isidatta, having declared his adherence to the Dhamma of the Blessed One, rose from his seat and
On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.

Then Citta the householder approached those elder bhikkhus; having approached, he paid homage to the elder bhikkhus and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Citta the householder said to the elder bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, may the elders consent to accept a meal from me tomorrow."
The elder bhikkhus consented by their silence.
Then Citta the householder, understanding the elders’ consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and keeping them to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the elder bhikkhus dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes, and—
They approached the householder Citta’s residence and, having arrived, sat down on the prepared seats.
Then the householder Citta approached the elder monks;
having approached and paid homage to the elder monks, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Citta said this to the venerable elder:
“‘The diversity of elements, the diversity of elements,’ venerable elder, it is said.
To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?
When this was said, the venerable elder remained silent.
A second time, the householder Citta said this to the venerable elder:
“Venerable elder, it is said: ‘the diversity of elements, the diversity of elements.
To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?”
A second time, the venerable elder remained silent.
A third time, Citta the householder said this to the venerable elder:
"Venerable elder, it is said: 'the diversity of elements, the diversity of elements.'"
“To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?
For a third time, the elder venerable one remained silent.
Now at that time, the venerable Isidatta was the most junior member of that community of bhikkhus.
Then the Venerable Isidatta said this to the Venerable Thera:
"Shall I answer this question for the householder Citta, venerable Thera?
"Answer it, friend Isidatta, for the householder Citta."
“Indeed, householder, you ask this:
‘Venerable elder, it is said, “the diversity of elements, the diversity of elements.
To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?’”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Householder, this is what has been called ‘the diversity of elements’ by the Blessed One:
the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element … [and so on] …”
“The mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
To this extent, householder, has the diversity of elements been taught by the Blessed One.
Then Citta the householder, having delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Isidatta’s words, personally served and satisfied the elder bhikkhus with excellent hard food and soft food.
Then the elder bhikkhus, having finished their meal and having removed their hands from their bowls, rose from their seats and departed.
Then the venerable elder said this to the venerable Isidatta:
"It was good, friend Isidatta, that this question occurred to you; this question did not occur to me."
"Therefore, friend Isidatta, whenever such a question as this should come up in another way, let that very same answer occur to you here.
The second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 41.3 (SN 41.3, PTS SN iv 285).
1. The Chapter on the Mind (Cittavagga). The Second Discourse to Isidatta.
At one time, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.

Then Citta the householder approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached and paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Citta the householder said this to the elder bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, may the elders consent to my meal tomorrow.
The elder bhikkhus consented by remaining silent.
Then Citta the householder, having understood the elders’ acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and keeping them to his right, departed.

Then, when that night had passed, the elder bhikkhus dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes, and went to the residence of Citta the householder. Having arrived, they sat down on the prepared seats.
Then Citta the householder approached the elder bhikkhus;
having approached and paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Citta the householder said this to the venerable elder:
"Venerable elder, as for these various kinds of views that arise in the world:..."

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is non-eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’—
or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
And as for these sixty-two views spoken of in the Brahmajāla Sutta— do these views,
venerable sir, arise when something exists, or do they not arise when that thing does not exist?”
When this was said, the venerable elder remained silent.
A second time, Citta the householder...
[as before] ...and a third time, Citta the householder said this to the venerable elder:
“Venerable elder, those various views that arise in the world—

such as ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ ‘the soul and the body are the same’ or ‘the soul and the body are different,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death’— ”
or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death";
or whatever these sixty-two views are that have been spoken of in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*;
“Venerable sir, upon the existence of what do these views arise, and upon the non-existence of what do they not arise?
For a third time, the elder venerable one remained silent.
Now at that time, the venerable Isidatta was the most junior member of that community of monks.
Then the Venerable Isidatta said this to the Venerable Thera:
"Shall I answer this question of the householder Citta, venerable Thera?
"Answer it, friend Isidatta, you shall answer this question of the householder Citta."
“Indeed, householder, you ask thus:
‘Venerable elder, as for these various views that arise in the world—
such as “the world is eternal,” or [as far as] “neither finite nor infinite”;’”
“Venerable sir, upon the existence of what do these views arise, and upon the non-existence of what do they not arise?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Gahapati, regarding these various kinds of views that arise in the world:”
‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite’;
‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’;
‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death.’
or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.

Furthermore, these sixty-two speculative views spoken of in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*—these views, householder, exist when the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) exists; they do not exist when the view of a personal body does not exist.”
“But how, venerable sir, does identity view arise?

“Here, householder, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
One regards feeling as self … perception … volitional formations … [and so on] … consciousness as self.
“One regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
In this way, householder, there is identity view.
“But how, venerable sir, does identity view not come to be?”
“Here, householder, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones;

who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-trained in the Dhamma of true persons—does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form. He does not regard feeling as self….”

He does not regard perception as self, nor self as possessing perception, nor perception as being in self, nor self as being in perception; he does not regard volitional formations as self... nor consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in self, nor self as being in consciousness.
“In this way, householder, the view of a personal body does not exist.
“Venerable sir, from where has Master Isidatta come?
“I have come from Avanti, householder.”
“Venerable sir, there is a clansman named Isidatta from Avanti who is a friend of ours though we have never met;
has he been seen by the Venerable One?
“Yes, householder,” [he replied].
“Venerable sir, where does that venerable one dwell at present?
When this was said, the venerable Isidatta remained silent.
“Is it that our noble Isidatta has passed away, venerable sir?”
“Yes, householder,” [he replied].
“May the venerable Isidatta take pleasure in Macchikāsaṇḍa, Bhante.
The Ambāṭaka Grove is delightful.”
“I shall make an effort for the noble Isidatta regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
“It is well said, householder,” he replied.

Then Citta the householder, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the words of the venerable Isidatta, personally served and satisfied the elder bhikkhus with excellent hard foods and soft foods.
Then the elder bhikkhus, having finished their meal and having put away their bowls and hands, rose from their seats and departed.
Then the venerable Thera said this to the venerable Isidatta:
"It was indeed well, friend Isidatta, that this question occurred to you."
“This question did not occur to me.
Therefore, friend Isidatta, whenever such a question should arise otherwise, that itself should occur to you here.
Then the Venerable Isidatta, having tidied his lodging, took his bowl and robe and departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa.
From the time he departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa, he remained thus departed; he did not return again.
This is the third [sutta]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 41.4 (SN 41.4, PTS SN iv 288).
1. The Chapter on the Mind (Cittavagga): The Discourse on the Great Miracle (Mahākāpāṭihāriyasutta).
On one occasion, a number of elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.

Then Citta the householder approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he paid homage to the elder bhikkhus and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Citta the householder said to the elder bhikkhus:
"Venerable sirs, may the elders consent to my offering a meal at the cow-pen tomorrow.
The elder bhikkhus consented by remaining silent.
Then Citta the householder, understanding the elders’ acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and keeping them to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the elder bhikkhus dressed in the morning, took their bowls and robes, and went to Citta’s cattle-pen. Having arrived, they sat down on the prepared seats.
Then the householder Citta, with his own hands, personally satisfied and served the elder bhikkhus with excellent ghee-porridge.
When the elder bhikkhus had finished eating and had set aside their bowls and washed their hands, they rose from their seats and departed.
The householder Citta, saying, "Dispose of the leftovers," followed closely behind the elder bhikkhus.
Now at that time it was hot and steaming;
those elder bhikkhus went along as if their bodies were melting, like those who have finished eating a meal.
At that time, the Venerable Mahaka was the youngest member of that Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then the Venerable Mahaka said this to the Venerable Thera:
“It would indeed be good, venerable Thera, if a cool breeze were to blow, if there were a gathering of clouds, and if the rain were to fall drop by drop.
“It would indeed be good, friend Mahaka, if a cool breeze were to blow, if there were a gathering of clouds, and if the rain were to fall drop by drop.”
Then the Venerable Mahaka performed such a feat of psychic power that a cool breeze blew, clouds gathered, and rain fell drop by drop.
Then it occurred to the householder Citta:
"Whosoever is the most junior monk in this Saṅgha of monks, such is his power of psychic transformation."
Then, having arrived at the monastery, the Venerable Mahaka said this to the Venerable Thera:
"Is that enough, venerable Thera?
"That is enough, friend Mahaka."
"To what extent, friend Mahaka, has loving-kindness been practiced? To what extent, friend Mahaka, has it been honored?
Then the elder bhikkhus went to their respective dwellings.
The Venerable Mahaka also went to his own dwelling.
Then the householder Citta approached the Venerable Mahaka;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Mahaka and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the householder Citta said this to the Venerable Mahaka:
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble Mahaka would show me a superhuman feat of psychic power.
“In that case, householder, spread out your upper robe on the veranda and strew a bundle of grass.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Citta the householder replied to the Venerable Mahaka, and having spread out his upper robe on the veranda, he strewed a bundle of grass.
Then the Venerable Mahaka entered the dwelling, closed the latch,
and performed such a feat of supernormal power that a flame emerged through the keyhole and the gap between the door panels,
burning the grass but not burning his upper robe.
Then Citta the householder, having shaken out his upper robe, stood to one side, agitated and with hair standing on end.
Then the Venerable Mahaka emerged from his dwelling and said this to Citta the householder:
“Is that enough, householder?”
“Enough, venerable Mahaka. This much is sufficient, venerable Mahaka. This much has been accomplished, venerable Mahaka. This much has been honored, venerable Mahaka.”
“May the venerable Mahaka take his pleasure in Macchikasaṇḍa, Bhante;
the Ambāṭaka Grove is delightful.
I shall exert myself on behalf of the venerable Mahaka regarding robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“‘The good is spoken of, householder,’ he said.
Then the Venerable Mahaka, having put away his lodging and taking his bowl and robe, departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa.
Once he had departed from Macchikāsaṇḍa, he remained departed.
But he did not return again.
This is the fourth [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 41.5 (SN 41.5, PTS SN iv 291).
1. The Chapter on Mind (Cittavagga).
Discourse on Kāmabhū the First (Paṭhamakāmabhūsutta).
At one time, the Venerable Kāmabhū was dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.
Then Citta the householder approached the Venerable Kāmabhū;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Kāmabhū and sat down to one side. As Citta the householder was sitting there, the Venerable Kāmabhū said this to him:
"This has been said, householder:"
‘A chariot with well-formed wheels, white canopy,
and a single axle rolls along;
see it approaching, free from distress.’
“‘With the stream cut, free from bonds’—
how, householder, should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?
“How was it, Bhante, that this was spoken by the Blessed One?”
“Yes, householder,” he replied.
“In that case, venerable sir, wait a moment while I consider its meaning.
Then Citta the householder, having remained silent for a moment, said this to the Venerable Kāmabhū:
“‘Nelaṅga,’ venerable sir, is a designation for the virtues.
‘White canopy,’ venerable sir, is a designation for liberation.
‘Eka,’ venerable sir, is a designation for mindfulness.”
“‘It rolls,’ venerable sir, is a designation for going forward and returning.

‘Chariot,’ venerable sir, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking up, and dissolution.
Lust, venerable sir, is a burden; hatred is a burden; delusion is a burden.”
For that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, these [afflictions] have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is called "one who is free from distress.
Furthermore, "the one who has gone" (*āyanta*), venerable sir, is a designation for an arahant.
“‘Stream,’ venerable sir, is a designation for craving.
That has been abandoned by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising.
Therefore, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is called ‘one whose stream is cut.’”
“Venerable sir, lust is a bond; hatred is a bond; delusion is a bond.
These have been abandoned by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more subject to future arising.
Therefore, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is called ‘one who is unbound.’”
Thus, venerable sir, as for that which was said by the Blessed One:
"The chariot with faultless limbs and a white canopy,
drawn by a single steed, rolls along."
“Behold him coming, free from distress,
with the stream cut off and unbound. This,
Bhante, is how I understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One in brief.”
“It is a gain for you, householder!
It is well-gained by you, householder, that your eye of wisdom ranges over the profound word of the Buddha.
The fifth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 41.6 (SN 41.6, PTS SN iv 293) 1. Cittavagga Dutiyakāmabhūsutta (The Second Discourse on Kāmabhū) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “The person who is like a stone statue; the person who is like a wooden statue; the person who is like a sandalwood statue; and the person who is like a golden statue. “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a stone statue? Here, someone is well-born on both sides, of pure maternal and paternal descent back to the seventh generation, unbroken, of flawless birth. But he is devoid of beauty, lacking in beauty; he is ugly, deformed, and unsightly. He is devoid of wealth, lacking in wealth; he is poor, indigent, and needy. And he is devoid of fame, lacking in fame; he is unknown, obscure, and insignificant. He is devoid of wisdom, lacking in wisdom; he is dull-witted, stupid, and slow to understand. This is called a person like a stone statue. “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a wooden statue? Here, someone is well-born... of flawless birth. He is endowed with beauty, possessing beauty; he is handsome, comely, and pleasing to look upon. But he is devoid of wealth... poor, indigent, and needy. And he is devoid of fame... unknown, obscure, and insignificant. He is devoid of wisdom... dull-witted, stupid, and slow to understand. This is called a person like a wooden statue. “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a sandalwood statue? Here, someone is well-born... of flawless birth. He is endowed with beauty... handsome, comely, and pleasing to look upon. He is endowed with wealth, possessing wealth; he is rich, affluent, and wealthy. But he is devoid of fame... unknown, obscure, and insignificant. He is devoid of wisdom... dull-witted, stupid, and slow to understand. This is called a person like a sandalwood statue. “And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a golden statue? Here, someone is well-born... of flawless birth. He is endowed with beauty... handsome, comely, and pleasing to look upon. He is endowed with wealth... rich, affluent, and wealthy. And he is endowed with fame, possessing fame; he is renowned, celebrated, and famous. He is endowed with wisdom, possessing wisdom; he is wise, intelligent, and sagacious. This is called a person like a golden statue. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
On one occasion the Venerable Kāmabhū was dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.
Then Citta the householder approached the Venerable Kāmabhū; having approached, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Citta the householder said this to the Venerable Kāmabhū:
"Venerable sir, how many formations are there?"
“There are, householder, three formations:
the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation.
“Excellent, venerable sir,” Citta the householder said, and having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Venerable Kāmabhū’s words, he asked the Venerable Kāmabhū a further question:
“But, Bhante, what is the bodily formation, what is the verbal formation, and what is the mental formation?
“Inhalation and exhalation, householder, are the bodily formation; applied thought and sustained thought are the verbal formation; perception and feeling are the mental formation.
“Excellent, Bhante! said Citta the householder... [and] asked a further question:

“But why, venerable sir, are in-breathing and out-breathing the bodily formation; why are applied thought and sustained thought the verbal formation; and why are perception and feeling the mental formation?
“In-breathing and out-breathing, householder, are physical. These phenomena are bound up with the body; therefore, in-breathing and out-breathing are the bodily formation.
First, householder, one applies thought and sustains thought, and afterwards one utters speech; therefore, applied thought and sustained thought are the verbal formation.”
“Perception and feeling are mental factors. These phenomena are bound to the mind; therefore, perception and feeling are formations of the mind.
“Excellent... [he said]... and asked a further question:
‘But how, venerable sir, does the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling come about?’”
“Householder, it does not occur to a bhikkhu entering the cessation of perception and feeling:
‘I will enter the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I am entering the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have entered the cessation of perception and feeling.
Rather, his mind has previously been developed in such a way that it leads him to that state.”
“Excellent... [as before] ... he asked a further question:
‘But, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, which phenomena cease first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?
‘For a bhikkhu, householder, who is attaining the cessation of perception and feeling, the verbal formation ceases first, then the bodily formation, and then the mental formation.’”
“Excellent... [as before] ... he asked a further question:
‘Venerable sir, what is the difference between one who is dead and passed away, and this bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling?
‘Householder, in the case of one who is dead and passed away, his bodily formations have ceased and subsided, his verbal formations...’”
The bodily formation has ceased and subsided; the mental formation has ceased and subsided; vitality is exhausted;
heat has been quenched; the faculties have become disintegrated.
And as for that monk, householder, who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, his bodily formation [is likewise stilled].
“Bodily formation has ceased and subsided; verbal formation has ceased and subsided; mental formation has ceased and subsided;
yet life is not exhausted, heat has not been quenched, and the faculties are serene.
Householder, this is the distinction between one who is dead and passed away, and this bhikkhu who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling.”
“Excellent... [as before] ... he asked a further question:
‘But, venerable sir, how does one emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?
‘Householder, it does not occur to a bhikkhu emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling:’”

‘I shall emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I am emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling,’ or ‘I have emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Yet his mind has already been developed beforehand in such a way that it leads him to that state.
“Excellent, venerable sir! ... [he said] ... and asked a further question:

“But for a bhikkhu, venerable sir, who is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which phenomena arise first: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, or the mental formation?

“For a bhikkhu, householder, who is emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, the mental formation arises first, then the bodily formation, and then the verbal formation.
“Excellent…” [and he said further: “…he asked another question:”
“But, venerable sir, how many kinds of contact touch a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?
“Householder, three kinds of contact touch a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling:
empty contact, signless contact, and desireless contact.”
“Excellent... [as before] ... he asked a further question:
‘But, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, to what does his mind incline, to what does it lean, to what does it tend?
‘Householder, for a bhikkhu who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, his mind inclines to seclusion, leans toward seclusion, and tends toward seclusion.’”
“Excellent, venerable sir! Citta the householder, having delighted and rejoiced in the Venerable Kāmabhū’s words, asked him a further question:
“But, venerable sir, how many things are of great assistance for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling?
“Certainly, householder, you ask what ought to be asked first.”
"Moreover, I shall explain this to you.
Householder, there are two things that are of great assistance for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling:
serenity and insight."
The Sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 41.7 (SN 41.7, PTS SN iv 295) 1.
Cittavagga (The Chapter on the Mind)
The Godatta Sutta.
On one occasion the Venerable Godatta was dwelling at Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Ambāṭaka Grove.
Then Citta the householder approached the Venerable Godatta; having approached, he [greeted] the Venerable...
Having paid homage to Godatta, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Godatta said this to the householder Citta:

"Householder, as for this immeasurable liberation of mind, this liberation of mind through nothingness, this liberation of mind through emptiness, and this signless liberation of mind—are these states different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and different only in phrasing?"
“Is it only the phrasing that is different?
“There is, Bhante, a method by which these states have both different meanings and different phrasing;
but there is also, Bhante, a method by which these states have the same meaning and only the phrasing is different.”
“And what, Bhante, is the method by means of which these states have different meanings and different expressions?
Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;
thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself...”
He dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on].
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… with a mind accompanied by equanimity,
he dwells pervading one direction, likewise the second, likewise the third,
likewise the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, in every way, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
This, venerable sir, is called the immeasurable liberation of mind.
And what, venerable sir, is the liberation of mind through nothingness?
"Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This, venerable sir, is called the mind-liberation of nothingness.
And what, venerable sir, is the mind-liberation of emptiness?"
"Here, Bhante, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
‘This is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self.
This, Bhante, is called the emptiness liberation of mind."
"And what, venerable sir, is the signless liberation of mind?
Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu, through non-attention to all signs, enters and dwells in the signless concentration of mind.
This, venerable sir, is called the signless liberation of mind."
"This, venerable sir, is the method by which these states have different meanings and different phrasing.
And what, venerable sir, is the method by which these states have the same meaning and differ only in phrasing?
Lust, venerable sir, is a maker of measure; hatred is a maker of measure; delusion is a maker of measure."
For that bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, these [defilements] have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
To whatever extent there are immeasurable liberations of mind, the unshakable liberation of mind is declared to be the foremost among them.
Furthermore, that unshakable liberation of mind is empty of lust, empty of hatred, and empty of delusion.
“Venerable sir, lust is a possession, hatred is a possession, and delusion is a possession.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, these have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising.
Venerable sir, among all the liberations of mind through nothingness, the unshakable liberation of mind is declared to be the foremost.”
Furthermore, that unshakable liberation of mind is empty of lust, empty of hatred, and empty of delusion.
Lust, venerable sir, creates signs; hatred creates signs; delusion creates signs.
For a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, these have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and are no longer subject to future arising.
"Venerable sir, to whatever extent there are signless liberations of mind, the unshakable liberation of mind is declared to be the foremost among them.
Furthermore, that unshakable liberation of mind is empty of lust, empty of hatred, and empty of delusion.
This, venerable sir, is the method by which, according to this method, these phenomena have the same meaning and differ only in expression."
“Gains for you, householder! Well-acquired by you, householder!
For your eye of wisdom ranges over the profound word of the Buddha.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 41.8 (SN 41.8, PTS SN iv 297) 1. Cittavagga The Discourse on Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on the past; the person who is intent on the future; the person who dwells with his mind bound by both the past and the future; and the person who dwells independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on the past? Here, bhikkhus, someone has acquired a certain view regarding the past, such as: ‘I existed in the past’ or ‘I did not exist in the past,’ or ‘I was something else in the past. He thinks about that very thing, contemplates it, and pursues it. This is called a person intent on the past. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person intent on the future? Here, bhikkhus, someone has acquired a certain view regarding the future, such as: ‘I will exist in the future’ or ‘I will not exist in the future,’ or ‘I will be something else in the future. He thinks about that very thing, contemplates it, and pursues it. This is called a person intent on the future. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who dwells with his mind bound by both the past and the future? Here, bhikkhus, someone has acquired a certain view regarding the past, such as: ‘I existed in the past’ or ‘I did not exist in the past,’ or ‘I was something else in the past. And he has acquired a certain view regarding the future, such as: ‘I will exist in the future’ or ‘I will not exist in the future,’ or ‘I will be something else in the future. He thinks about that very thing, contemplates it, and pursues it. This is called a person who dwells with his mind bound by both the past and the future. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who dwells independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called a person who dwells independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. In what respect, venerable sir, is he called ‘the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta’? “Ānanda, Nātaputta is his family name, and because he is a Nigaṇṭha, he is called ‘the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. “But, venerable sir, why is he called a ‘Nigaṇṭha’? “Ānanda, whatever evil deeds were done by Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta through body, speech, or mind, he has shaken them off, washed them away, released them, and let them go. Therefore, Ānanda, he is called a ‘Nigaṇṭha. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are Nigaṇṭhas too? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have shaken off, washed away, released, and let go of evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind. Therefore, they too are called ‘Nigaṇṭhas. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are not Nigaṇṭhas? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have not shaken off, washed away, released, or let go of evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind. Therefore, they are not called ‘Nigaṇṭhas. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are both Nigaṇṭhas and not Nigaṇṭhas? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have shaken off, washed away, released, and let go of some evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, but have not yet done so for others.

Therefore, they are both called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ and ‘not Nigaṇṭhas. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are neither Nigaṇṭhas nor not Nigaṇṭhas? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have neither shaken off, washed away, released, nor let go of any evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind. Therefore, they are neither called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ nor ‘not Nigaṇṭhas. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are Nigaṇṭhas and who have attained peace of mind? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have shaken off, washed away, released, and let go of evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, and who dwell independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. Therefore, they are called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ and ‘those who have attained peace of mind. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are not Nigaṇṭhas but have attained peace of mind? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have not shaken off, washed away, released, or let go of evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, yet dwell independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. Therefore, they are not called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ but are called ‘those who have attained peace of mind. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are both Nigaṇṭhas and have attained peace of mind, and who are also not Nigaṇṭhas but have attained peace of mind? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have shaken off, washed away, released, and let go of some evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, and who dwell independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind; while others have not shaken off, washed away, released, or let go of any evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, yet dwell independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. Therefore, they are both called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ and ‘those who have attained peace of mind,’ and also ‘not Nigaṇṭhas’ and ‘those who have attained peace of mind. “But, venerable sir, does Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta have any disciples who are neither Nigaṇṭhas nor have attained peace of mind? “There are, Ānanda, some disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta who have neither shaken off, washed away, released, nor let go of any evil deeds done through body, speech, and mind, and who do not dwell independent of both the past and the future, not clinging, not grasping, having attained peace of mind. Therefore, they are neither called ‘Nigaṇṭhas’ nor ‘those who have attained peace of mind. “But, venerable sir, does
Now at that time, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta had arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
Citta the householder heard: "The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has indeed arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
Then Citta the householder, accompanied by several lay followers, approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As the householder Citta was sitting there, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said this to him:
"Householder, do you have faith in the ascetic Gotama that there is a concentration free from directed thought and evaluation, and that there is the cessation of directed thought and evaluation?"
“Venerable sir, it is not out of faith in the Blessed One that I say this:
there is a concentration without directed thought and evaluation; there is the cessation of directed thought and evaluation.
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta looked up and said this:
“Sirs, look at this: how straightforward this householder Citta is, how honest this householder Citta is, how free from deceit this householder Citta is!
He who would think that initial and sustained thought should be suppressed would be like one who thinks to obstruct the wind with a net;
he who would think that the current of the Ganges should be dammed up with his own fist—[he would be like him].”
“Whoever would conceive that applied thought and sustained thought are to be ceased, they would conceive thus.
“What do you think, Bhante, which is more excellent: knowledge or faith?”
“Householder, knowledge is indeed more excellent than faith.

“Venerable sir, as much as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
Venerable sir, as much as I wish, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I enter and dwell in the second jhāna...”
"Venerable sir, as much as I wish, with the fading away of rapture... I enter and dwell in the third jhāna.
Venerable sir, as much as I wish, with the abandoning of pleasure... I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna.
Knowing and seeing thus, venerable sir, on whose faith would I go—to what other ascetic or brahmin?"
“There is concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought; there is the cessation of directed thought and sustained thought.
When this was said, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta looked toward his own assembly and said:
“Sirs, look at how crooked this householder Citta is! Look at how fraudulent this householder Citta is! Look at how deceitful this householder Citta is!”
“Just now, Bhante, we spoke thus:
‘May you see this: how upright this householder Citta is, how honest this householder Citta is, how free from deceit this householder Citta is.
And yet, Bhante, just now we have spoken thus:”
“We understand it thus, sirs; please see for yourselves: how straightforward this householder Citta is, how fraudulent this householder Citta is, and how deceitful this householder Citta is.
“Venerable sir, if your former statement is true, your latter one is false.
But if, venerable sir, your former statement is false, your latter one is true.”
"Furthermore, Bhante, these ten questions consistent with the Dhamma come to me.
When you understand their meaning, then you may respond to me in the presence of the assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
There is one question, one summary, and one exposition."
Two questions, two indications, two explanations.
Three questions, three indications, three explanations.
Four questions, four indications, four explanations.
Five questions, five summaries, five explanations.
Six questions, six summaries, six explanations.
Seven questions, seven summaries, seven explanations.
Eight questions, eight summaries, and eight explanations.
Nine questions, nine summaries, and nine explanations.
Ten questions, ten summaries, and ten explanations.”
Then Citta the householder, having asked the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta these ten questions on matters of the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
This was the eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 41.9 (SN 41.9, PTS SN iv 300).
Now at that time, the naked ascetic Kassapa had arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa; he was an old lay friend of the householder Citta.
The householder Citta heard: “It is said that the naked ascetic Kassapa has arrived at Macchikāsaṇḍa;
he was formerly a companion of mine from my lay life. Then the householder Citta approached the naked ascetic Kassapa; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the naked ascetic Kassapa.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Citta said this to the naked ascetic Kassapa:
“How long has it been since you went forth, venerable Kassapa?
“For about thirty years, householder, it has been since I went forth.
“But during these thirty years, venerable sir, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a dwelling in comfort?”
“Householder, during these thirty years since I went forth, I have not attained any superhuman state,
any distinction in noble knowledge and vision, or any state of comfort, other than nakedness, shaven-headedness,
and the rubbing of my body with ashes.”
When this was said, the householder Citta said to the naked ascetic Kassapa:
“It is wonderful, sir! It is marvelous, sir!
How well-proclaimed is the Dhamma, in that for thirty years no one has ever surpassed human norms.”
“If this noble distinction of knowledge and vision had been attained, it would have been a comfortable dwelling, were it not for the state of being naked, shaven-headed,
and the practice of rubbing with pebbles.
“But for how long, householder, have you been one who has approached the status of a lay follower?”
“Venerable sir, it has been thirty years since I entered upon the status of a lay follower.
“But, householder, during these thirty years, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision, or a comfortable dwelling?
“It may well be so, venerable sir, even for a householder.”

“Indeed, venerable sir, whenever I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

Indeed, venerable sir, whenever I wish, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, I enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration.

Indeed, venerable sir, whenever I wish, with the fading away as well of rapture, I enter and dwell in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.’”
“Venerable sir, as soon as I wish, by the abandoning of pleasure... I enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna.
But if, venerable sir, I were to pass away before the Blessed One, it would not be surprising if the Blessed One were to declare of me:
‘There is no fetter bound by which the householder Citta might return again to this world.’”
When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the householder Citta:
“It is wonderful, indeed, sir! It is marvelous, indeed, sir!
How well-proclaimed is the Dhamma, in that a white-robed householder can attain such a distinction of superhuman states, a noble distinction of knowledge and vision, and a state of easeful dwelling.”
“Householder, may I receive the going-forth in this Dhamma and Discipline? May I receive the full ordination?
Then Citta the householder, taking the naked ascetic Kassapa with him, approached the elder bhikkhus; having approached, he said to the elder bhikkhus:
“Venerable sirs, this naked ascetic Kassapa was formerly a lay friend of ours.”
"Let the elders grant him the going-forth and the full ordination.
I shall provide for his requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick.
Thus, the naked ascetic Kassapa received the going-forth in this Dhamma and Vinaya; he received the full ordination.
And not long after his full ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Kassapa,

by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
“Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”—thus he directly knew.
And the Venerable Kassapa became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 41.10 (SN 41.10, PTS SN iv 302) 1. Cittavagga Gilānadassanasutta — The Discourse on Visiting the Sick At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, visit the sick. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Then they went to the sick person and said: “Friend, the Blessed One says this to you: ‘Come, friend, do not be afraid. You will not die here, friend; you will not pass away here. When they had spoken thus, the sick person said to them: “Friends, I am not afraid. Why should I be afraid? For I have heard from the Blessed One’s own lips: ‘Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, friends, one person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. Here, friends, another person is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. Here, friends, still another person is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And here, friends, yet another person is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “Of these, friends, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is the one who has entered upon the way leading to his own welfare, but has not yet entered upon the way leading to the welfare of others. The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is the one who has entered upon the way leading to the welfare of others, but has not yet entered upon the way leading to his own welfare. The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is the one who has not entered upon the way leading to his own welfare, nor has he entered upon the way leading to the welfare of others. But the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is the one who has entered upon the way leading to his own welfare, and has also entered upon the way leading to the welfare of others. “Now, friends, I am one who is intent on my own welfare and on the welfare of others. For I have abandoned the five lower fetters and I am one bound upstream, heading toward the Akaniṭṭha realm. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, when a person has been visited by the sick, it is proper for him to say: ‘Friend, have you attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your destination? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question either, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your view? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question either, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your inclination? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question either, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your conviction? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question either, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your refuge? “If, bhikkhus, the sick person does not answer when asked this question either, he should be asked again: ‘Friend, what is your reliance? Now at that time, the householder Citta was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.

Then many deities dwelling in groves, deities dwelling in woods, deities dwelling in trees, and deities inhabiting medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest thickets, having gathered and assembled together, said this to the householder Citta:
"Make a resolve, householder, for the future: 'May I become a wheel-turning monarch!'"
When this was said, Citta the householder said this to those deities dwelling in the groves, the woods, the trees, and the medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants:
"That too is impermanent; that too is unstable; that too must be abandoned and departed from.
When this was said, Citta the householder’s friends, colleagues, kinsmen, and blood relations said this to Citta the householder:
“Establish mindfulness, noble son; do not prattle on.
“What am I saying that you say to me:
‘Establish mindfulness, noble son; do not prattle on’?”
“Noble son, you say:
‘That too is impermanent, that too is unstable, that too must be abandoned and departed from.
“But it was because the deities of the groves, the deities of the woods, the deities of the trees, and the deities dwelling in the medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants spoke thus to me:”
“‘Make a vow, householder, that in a future time you shall be a wheel-turning monarch.
To that I say:
‘That too is impermanent... [and so on] ... even that must be abandoned and departed from.’”

“But why, noble son, did those deities of the groves, the deities of the woods, the deities of the trees, and the deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants speak thus, seeing some purpose:
‘Make a wish, householder, for the future: may you become a wheel-turning monarch’?
“It occurred to those deities of the groves, the deities of the woods, the deities of the trees, and the deities dwelling in medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest giants as follows:”
“This householder Citta is virtuous and of beautiful character.
If he should make the aspiration:
‘In a future time, may I be a wheel-turning monarch,’ then this will indeed succeed for him; for the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous, being pure, observes its own lawful fruit.”
"Indeed, those deities dwelling in the groves, the forest deities, the tree deities, and the deities inhabiting medicinal herbs, grasses, and forests, seeing a certain purpose, spoke thus:
'Householder, make a resolution that in a future time you shall be a wheel-turning monarch.
To them, I say this:"
“‘That too is impermanent, that too is unstable, that too must be abandoned and departed from.
“In that case, noble son, please instruct us as well.
“Therefore, you should train yourselves thus:”
We shall be endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, [thinking]:

"Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
We shall be endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma...
‘The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
We shall be endowed with unwavering confidence in the Sangha:

‘The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the straight way, the Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the true way...’
‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing rightly;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples consists of these four pairs of persons, these eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’”

"Furthermore, whatever gift-worthy property there may be in the family, all of that shall be shared without distinction with those who are virtuous and of good character"—thus indeed should you train yourselves.
Then Citta the householder, having exhorted his friends, colleagues, relatives, and kinsmen in the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and in generosity, passed away.
The Tenth.
The first chapter is the Cittavagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
Saṃyojana, the two Isidattās.
Mahaka and Kāmabhū,
Godatta and the Nigaṇṭha,
and the visit to the sick man with Acela.
The Connected Discourses on the Mind are complete.
